lead: Every open-loop transfer function carries two labels that decide different things. The order counts the poles, so it sets how many natural modes shape the transient. The type counts only the poles at s = 0, so it sets the steady-state error for a step, ramp or parabola. A designer uses type to meet an accuracy target and order to know what transient to expect. In a motor position loop, a type-1 open loop gives zero step error; the order tells whether the response has one time constant or a ringing second-order pair.
prereq: You need Unit 1 transfer functions and Chapter 2.1 for step, ramp and parabola inputs.

blocks.text: Write the open-loop transfer function of a unity feedback system in pole-zero form: G(s) = K(s+z₁)(s+z₂)… / [s<sup>N</sup>(s+p₁)(s+p₂)…]. Here G(s) is the forward-path transfer function when the feedback path is H(s)=1; s is the Laplace variable in s⁻¹; K is the gain; z₁, z₂, … are the magnitudes of the zeros, so G(s)=0 at s = −z₁, −z₂, …; p₁, p₂, … are the magnitudes of the nonzero poles, so the nonzero poles sit at s = −p₁, −p₂, …; N is the number of poles at s = 0. A factor (s+3) means a zero of magnitude 3 at s = −3, and (s+5) means a pole of magnitude 5 at s = −5. A pole at s = 0 is an integrator, because 1/s integrates in time.

The order n is the degree of the denominator after cancelling common factors. Equivalently, n = N + number of nonzero poles. The type N is the number of poles at s = 0. Some syllabi call it system type or error type.

items: Type 0, order 2: G(s)=10/[(s+2)(s+5)]. No origin pole; two nonzero poles.
Type 1, order 2: G(s)=4/[s(s+3)]. One origin pole; one nonzero pole.
Type 2, order 4: G(s)=20(s+3)/[s²(s+1)(s+5)]. Two origin poles; two nonzero poles.
Type 3, order 4: G(s)=7/[s³(s+1)]. Three origin poles; one nonzero pole.

blocks.text: For a non-unity feedback system with forward path G(s) and feedback H(s), the error transfer function is E(s)/R(s)=1/[1+G(s)H(s)]. Write the equivalent open-loop (loop-gain) transfer function G(s)H(s) and count type and order from it, not from G(s) alone. Type fixes steady-state error; order fixes the transient shape.

The time-constant form pulls the pole and zero magnitudes out of the factors: G(s) = K′(1+sT₁)(1+sT₂)… / [s<sup>N</sup>(1+sT<sub>a</sub>)(1+sT<sub>b</sub>)…]. K′ is the time-constant gain; T₁, T₂, … are zero time constants, with T₁=1/z₁, T₂=1/z₂, … in seconds when z is in rad/s; T<sub>a</sub>, T<sub>b</sub>, … are nonzero pole time constants, with T<sub>a</sub>=1/p<sub>a</sub>, … in seconds when p is in rad/s. Pulling out the magnitudes gives K′ = K z₁ z₂ … / (p₁ p₂ …). In this gain formula, z and p are magnitudes. So K and K′ differ by the product of zero magnitudes divided by the product of nonzero pole magnitudes. The s<sup>N</sup> stays outside because origin poles have no finite time constant.

For G(s)=20(s+3)/[s²(s+1)(s+5)], K′=20×3/(1×5)=12, and G(s)=12(1+s/3)/[s²(1+s)(1+s/5)] = 12(1+0.333s)/[s²(1+s)(1+0.2s)]. The time constants are 0.333 s, 1 s and 0.2 s. For type 0, K′ equals G(0), the DC gain. For type 1 and higher, G(0) is infinite, so K′ is not a DC gain. Use K′ when you read a Bode plot; use K when you count gain in pole-zero form. The error constants in Chapter 2.6 take their own limits.

Type and order are read from the open-loop transfer function, not from the closed-loop one. They describe the plant plus controller before feedback closes. Adding an integrator in a PI controller raises the type by one. On a type-0 plant this removes the step error; on a type-1 plant it removes the ramp error. Either way it adds phase lag and eats phase margin. Adding a pole raises order, for example a motor's electrical time constant or a filter, so the transient gains one more mode. A distant pole contributes a small, fast decay and may be ignored as a dominant-pole approximation. A higher type is not automatically better: each origin pole adds 90° of phase lag, and stability must be checked in Unit 3. The labels are bookkeeping: type answers 'what error remains?', order answers 'what transient shape is possible?'. They also tell you which response formula to use: one time constant in Chapter 2.3, two in Chapter 2.4.

spec.aria: A tree splits the worked-example open-loop transfer function G(s) into order 4 from the denominator degree and type 2 from the two poles at the origin.

examples.question: For G(s) = 20(s+3)/[s²(s+1)(s+5)], find the order, the type, and the time-constant form.
steps: Denominator: s²(s+1)(s+5). Its degree is 2 + 1 + 1 = 4, so the order is n = 4.
Origin poles: s² gives two poles at s = 0, so the type is N = 2.
Common factors: numerator has s+3; denominator has s, s, s+1, s+5. No common factor cancels, so order and type stay 4 and 2.
Zero time constant: zero at s = −3 gives T = 1/3 s ≈ 0.333 s.
Nonzero pole time constants: pole at s = −1 gives T = 1 s; pole at s = −5 gives T = 0.2 s.
Gain: K = 20, zero magnitude product = 3, nonzero pole magnitude product = 1 × 5 = 5. K′ = 20 × 3 / 5 = 12.
examples.answer: The system has order 4, type 2, time-constant gain K′ = 12, and time constants 0.333 s, 1 s and 0.2 s.
examples.check:
order = 2 + 1 + 1
type_n = 2
K = 20
Kp = K * 3 / (1 * 5)
T1 = 1 / 3
T2 = 1 / 1
T3 = 1 / 5
print(order)
print(type_n)
print(int(Kp))
print(round(T1, 3))
print(int(T2))
print(round(T3, 3))

traps: Counting every pole for type. Type counts only poles at s = 0, not poles at s = −1, −2 or −5.
Treating a small negative pole as an origin pole. A pole at s = −0.001 is not an integrator; it is type 0, though it can cause a slow tail.
Forgetting to cancel common factors before finding order. A factor s+a in both numerator and denominator lowers the true order by one.
Reading type and order from the closed-loop denominator or from G(s) alone in non-unity feedback. Use the loop gain G(s)H(s).
Mixing K and K′. K′ includes the product of zero magnitudes divided by the product of nonzero pole magnitudes.

quiz.q: Define order and type of an open-loop transfer function.
quiz.a: Order n is the degree of the denominator after cancelling common factors. Type N is the number of poles at s = 0.

quiz.q: Why does a zero not change the order or the type?
quiz.a: A zero is a root of the numerator. Order comes from the denominator degree, and type counts denominator roots at s = 0. A zero changes the gain and phase shape, not those two counts.

quiz.q: For G(s)=8(s+1)/[s(s+2)(s+4)], find the order, type and K′.
quiz.a: Denominator degree = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so order = 3. One pole at s = 0, so type = 1. K′ = 8 × 1 / (2 × 4) = 1.

quiz.q: Two systems both have order 3. System A is type 0; system B is type 1. Which has zero steady-state error to a step, and why?
quiz.a: System B. A type-1 open loop has one integrator, so the step error is zero. A type-0 system has finite nonzero step error.

quiz.q: For G(s)=15/[s²(s+3)(s+5)], write the time-constant form and K′.
For a non-unity feedback system, what must be done before reading type and order?
quiz.a: Write the loop-gain transfer function G(s)H(s); count type and order from it, not from G(s) alone. The error transfer is E(s)/R(s)=1/[1+G(s)H(s)].

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, type and order are the first two numbers written on a loop datasheet: type sets the integral action needed for zero steady-state error, order sets the model size used in simulation. Modern software identifies poles and zeros from measured frequency response, then reports type and order automatically. Researchers use fractional-order and higher-order models when a simple integer type fails to fit a slow tail. Search for 'system type steady-state error', 'pole-zero cancellation', and 'fractional-order control'.
